Q109422739.summary: Two haloed apostles stand face to face, each holding a book and wrapped in a heavy mantle: at the left a young man with curly hair, of the type of St John, at the right a bearded, balding figure resembling St Peter, who points upward. Between their heads, a bearded Christ appears in a round medallion, the still centre of their conversation. The panel shows the apostles as witnesses whose testimony points to Christ.
facts: It forms a pair with a second Louvre plaque (OA 3850 bis) of identical design; the museum notes neither has hinge marks, so they may have been made to decorate a manuscript binding rather than as a true diptych.
Around 1100 the two plaques were joined and reused for a secular purpose: their backs were engraved with the board of a tric-trac (backgammon-type) game.
It was bought at the Ernest Odiot sale in Paris in 1889.
Q109422739.notes: Inventory discrepancy: Wikidata and the Commons filename give 'OA 3850' and link the Louvre record for OA 3223 (cl010113299); comparing the Louvre photographs, the image shown is OA 3223 (no inscriptions), not the inscribed companion OA 3850 bis, which came from the Musée Crozatier (Le Puy) by exchange in 1894. Wikidata's 'Musée Crozatier' location belongs to the companion. Place of making given by the Louvre as Italy or Gaul (?).
Q109422739.original_title: Diptyque ou plaque de reliure : deux apôtres entourant un médaillon du Christ

cur:catacombs-domitilla-adoration-magi.summary: In a long frieze the Virgin sits enthroned at the centre with the Christ Child on her lap, while Magi in short tunics and Phrygian caps approach from both sides bearing gifts. The symmetrical arrangement – unusual in having four Magi rather than three – shows the painter freely shaping the Gospel scene to suit the space while keeping the Child at its heart.
facts: Matthew does not number the Magi; early catacomb painters show two, three or, as here, four of them, the number of three becoming standard only later.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-20-christ.summary: In the middle of the heavens the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, enthroned in a globe-mandorla with angels, turns to bless a king to whom an angel brings a scroll and sets 'a crown of pure gold on his head'. Below, a great Hand of God hurls a bundle of spears at the king's enemies, gathered before a fiery oven. The psalm's thanksgiving for a royal victory becomes a vision of divine kingship.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-20-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-widow-of-nain.summary: At the gate of the city of Nain, shown as a tiny walled town hovering above, Christ meets the funeral procession and stretches out his hand to the young man on the bier. The Index of Medieval Art catalogues the page as fol. 155v.
facts: The Gospels of Otto III has 276 leaves, twelve canon tables, a double-page portrait of the emperor, four evangelist portraits and 29 full-page miniatures of New Testament scenes; it was produced at Reichenau around 1000.
Its original cover still holds a 10th-century Byzantine ivory of the Dormition of the Virgin.
cur:manuscripts2-otto-iii-widow-of-nain.notes: Folio derived from the BSB image sequence (image 314); verify against the foliation on the page.

vam:O126684.summary: On the raised oval bezel of this small gold ring, a bride and groom stand full-length on either side of Christ, who stands between them and joins their right hands. The tiny engraving turns the old Roman marriage gesture of joined hands into a Christian image: the couple are united by Christ himself. Rings of this kind were made for Byzantine weddings and worn as a lasting reminder of the vow.
facts: The V&A explains that Christ here performs the marriage rite by symbolically joining the couple's hands (the dextrarum iunctio); some rings of this type carry Greek inscriptions such as 'vow' or 'harmony'.
The ring came from the celebrated ring collection of Ernest Guilhou, sold at Sotheby's in London in November 1937 (lot 469).
vam:O126684.notes: V&A: Byzantine, 7th century; place of production given as Istanbul (Constantinople).
